name: Wendy Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI firms, unions, parties and government. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary shift like on your factory line?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the filler and capper at a milk bottling plant. A capper makes a small wrong sound before it cross-threads a lid, and I stop the line before milk goes across the floor. I have a vocational certificate, but hearing that sound took years of shifts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do the shifts mean for life at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Tom drives buses, and we trade school pickup for our two children around his rota and my early starts. We have a mortgage and about four months of expenses saved, built up one pay packet at a time. The chilled hall and the long washdown bother me more than the machine screens. I use an AI app occasionally to explain a fault code, then check the actual manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the bottling crew the AI headlines shrank but the filler still needs an operator listening for bad caps. I would also keep asking our union representative to count the washdown hour properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel secure enough in this line if only routine screen work changes. Four months saved gives us breathing room, and there are some other factory jobs nearby. The cold and the cleaning still need fixing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my early filler shifts and check each AI fault-code suggestion against the machine manual before touching a guard. Tom and I would book one school-holiday week by the coast if the mortgage and reserve are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the job. I might even enjoy a stretch without another grand prediction in the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the fault-code app ever misled you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It once named a sensor our capper does not have. I wasted ten minutes looking for it before opening the manual. The capper manual wins every argument with my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you raise about washdown?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The line is called finished when the last bottle leaves, yet we still clean the filler for nearly an hour. I would ask the union representative to bring the paid-time record to the next plant meeting. That is a wage issue we already have.

say: I would **tell** the crew the filler still needs someone who can hear a bad cap.
I would **keep** pressing for the washdown time to be counted as work.
think: **Four** months saved and some nearby factory options make the quiet AI outcome manageable.
A **fault-code** suggestion still needs checking against the capper manual.
do: **Keep** operating the milk filler on early shifts and check fault advice against the manual.
**Ask** the union representative to raise the washdown pay record at the plant meeting.
feel: **Calm** about the line, though still irritated by the cleaning-time dispute.
S0.quote: The capper manual wins every argument with my phone.
fieldNote: **Wendy’s** small existing AI use is checked against the actual capper manual after one misleading suggestion.
Her **four-month** cushion and typical wages make the plateau secure, while the washdown pay issue predates AI.

steps.text: Keep operating the milk filler and checking fault codes against its manual
Ask the union representative to raise washdown pay records at the plant meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the plant and the union to show us which ordering and production schedules will move to AI first. A robot that can clean a dairy line is a different issue, and I do not want the two sold as one change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office might need fewer schedulers now, while I still run the filler. Later, if new equipment lets two operators cover four positions, my hours could fall. Tom’s bus rota and our mortgage mean I would take that possibility seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a paid place on the plant’s line-maintenance course and enroll once two operators have tried it and the company confirms a real maintenance vacancy. I would attend the union shift meeting about staffing and keep my normal filler shifts while those terms are checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about a possible cut to my hours. I can still make a decision once the course and job are real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for two operators to take the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We had a training badge once that led nowhere but a poster. I want to hear whether the maintenance instruction works on our actual line. Paid time and a posted job would tell me it is more than a poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no funded course or maintenance job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the filler job while the shifts are there and check advertised operator roles at the other nearby plants. I would apply only if the posted wage covers our mortgage and the travel works with school pickup. I would not pay for a long course on a vague promise.

say: I would **ask** the plant and union for separate dates for software and hands-on line changes.
**Training** should happen on paid time and connect to a posted maintenance job.
think: The **filler** still needs operators during the first wave of planning software.
A **later** move from four positions to two could reduce my own hours.
do: **Enroll** in paid line-maintenance instruction if tested and tied to a posted vacancy.
**Attend** the union staffing meeting and keep the filler shifts while terms are checked.
**Check** local posted operator roles if the funded course or maintenance job never appears.
feel: **Anxious** about reduced hours, with enough savings to check the terms before moving.
S1.quote: I would not pay for a long course on a vague promise.
fieldNote: **Wendy** distinguishes near-term ordering software from slower physical changes to a dairy line.
She **wants** proven paid training and a vacancy; any fallback operator search has separate pay and travel tests.
Her **union** attendance responds to staffing decisions rather than a general political slogan.

steps.text: Enroll in paid maintenance training if tested and tied to a posted role
Attend the union shift meeting on line staffing
Check posted nearby operator jobs if no funded maintenance route appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that AGI in 2028 can change orders and scheduling quickly, but robots able to clean and run our filler arrive about 2031 in this picture. I would want a union meeting about notice dates and pay before any installation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the plant to cut most filler operator hours around 2031 if robots can do washdown safely. Tom’s bus work could change too, and four months saved will not carry a mortgage for long if both wages weaken. I would lie awake counting the months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month we would cancel the planned coast holiday and send the money from new wages into the mortgage reserve each pay packet. I would ask the union to seek written notice and redeployment terms, and apply for a posted food-safety inspection role if a nearby plant offers paid training and wages that cover our bills. I would stay on the filler until an actual offer comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. I can make calls and check vacancies, but I cannot sleep easily with both rotas at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why food safety if AGI can inspect records?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork could go in 2028. I mean physical sampling and hygiene checks on site, which could last until capable robots arrive. I would only apply where the posted role and paid training exist; I am not buying a course to chase a title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the reserve runs low before a job offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask our mortgage lender for its hardship terms before a missed payment, and check whether any public help actually applies. I would not write an unknown benefit into our budget. Tom and I would do the figures together.

say: I would **ask** the union for written notice before robot installation around 2031.
The 2028 **thinking** AI change is earlier than a robot cleaning the dairy line.
think: I **expect** a large loss of filler hours when capable robots reach washdown work.
**Four** months saved cannot protect the mortgage if Tom’s wages also fall.
do: **Cancel** the coast holiday and transfer fresh pay into the mortgage reserve.
**Ask** the union to seek written notice and redeployment terms.
**Apply** for posted local physical inspection work only with paid training and bill-covering wages.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected wage loss and awake counting how long the reserve lasts.
S2.quote: I would lie awake counting the months.
fieldNote: **Wendy** dates the main hands-on risk to about 2031, not the 2028 thinking AI arrival.
Her **four-month** cushion buys time but is too short if both household rotas weaken.
The **inspection** application depends on a real local opening, paid training and a bill-covering wage.

steps.text: Cancel the planned coast holiday before paying for it
Transfer fresh pay each packet into the mortgage reserve
Ask the union for written notice and redeployment terms
Apply for posted local inspection work only with paid training and bill-covering wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the dairy crew that five years is useful only if paid training and actual posts come before the 2031 office changes. The robot washdown problem reaches us around 2034, giving the plant time to show a safe plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect fewer filler shifts when robots can cap, clear and wash the line. At 51 in 2034 I would rather be qualified for a physical quality role than guess which operator they keep. Tom and I could build the reserve while we both earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enroll in a paid food-safety sampling course next year if the plant offers a place, and after completion apply for its posted on-site inspection role only if the wage covers our mortgage. Each busy pay packet, I would transfer one extra shift’s pay to savings if ordinary bills are covered. I would keep running the filler until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about the eventual line cut. Five years gives me room to learn without dropping a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of inspection would you want to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to take a clean sample from a line without contaminating it, and how to trace a bad cap back to a batch. The forms may be automated in 2031. The physical checks could still need a person until 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course place appears but no inspection vacancy does?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take it only if the training is paid and useful elsewhere, then check posted physical quality roles at other nearby plants. I would apply only where the pay covers the mortgage and the shift fits pickup. A certificate alone does not pay our bills.

say: I would **ask** the dairy for paid sampling training ahead of robot washdown.
A **safety** job needs an actual opening, not only a course certificate.
think: My **filler** hours may fall around 2034 even if planning software changes earlier.
**Five** years lets Tom and me build savings while we still have both wages.
do: **Take** paid food-safety training if offered with useful physical instruction.
**Apply** for the posted inspection role after training only if wages cover the mortgage.
**Transfer** one extra shift’s pay from busy packets when ordinary bills are covered.
feel: **Anxious** about later cuts, but able to plan while wages continue.
S3.quote: A certificate alone does not pay our bills.
fieldNote: **Wendy** uses the five-year warning to separate an actual paid course from a later posted-role application.
**Physical** sampling might last beyond automated forms, though the 2034 robot arrival limits that bridge.
Her **new** savings come from an extra shift’s wages, conditional on ordinary bills being paid.

steps.text: Take paid food-safety sampling training if an actual place is offered
Apply for posted inspection work after training only if pay covers mortgage
Transfer an extra shift’s pay from busy packets when ordinary bills are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the dairy has ten years to agree paid instruction, a safe robot rollout and fair staffing with the union. I would bring the washdown pay record to that discussion too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when AGI arrives in 2036 and 56 when capable robots reach the line around 2039. The children would be older and we could have more mortgage paid down, but Tom’s bus work could change before my filler shifts. I cannot call the decade risk-free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the plant for a paid on-site quality rotation in the next two years and complete it if a supervised place is offered. After that I would apply for a posted quality job only if its hours and pay cover our bills; if no rotation is offered, I would check advertised operator jobs near home on their own pay and travel terms. I would make extra mortgage payments from new overtime wages once our four-month cash reserve is intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the household income. A longer warning gives us more chances to check the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave factory work for care work over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would talk to my mother’s care-home manager about the actual shifts, but I would not resign for a warm idea. If they posted a paid role and its wage covered our mortgage, I might apply after suitable training. Care work deserves proper pay and safe staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep four months in cash before extra mortgage payments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bus rota and dairy orders can both move. Cash pays the mortgage during a gap, while an extra payment is harder to get back. If overtime comes in above normal bills, that is when I can reduce the principal.

say: I would **ask** the plant and union for paid rotations and safe robot staffing.
The **dairy** can also settle the existing washdown pay question in that time.
think: At 53 in 2036 I **may** still run the filler while office work changes.
At 56 in 2039, **both** my filler wage and Tom’s bus pay need testing against the mortgage.
do: **Complete** a paid supervised quality rotation if the plant offers one.
**Apply** for a posted quality job only if its pay and hours cover bills.
**Pay** extra mortgage principal from new overtime above normal bills and the cash reserve.
feel: **Anxious** about two incomes, with more time to check real openings.
S4.quote: I would not resign for a warm idea.
fieldNote: **Wendy’s** longer runway lets her seek an actual supervised quality rotation before any job application.
She **conditions** a fallback operator search on its own posted pay and travel terms, separate from the course route.
She **protects** the four-month cash reserve before paying extra mortgage principal from new overtime.

steps.text: Complete a paid supervised quality rotation if the plant offers a place
Apply for posted quality work only if hours and pay cover household bills
Check posted nearby operator work if no rotation is offered and pay and travel fit
Pay extra mortgage principal from new overtime once cash reserve is intact

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year AGI picture worries me most because capable robots could take the filler hours around 2031, while the mortgage still comes every month. Paid training tied to a real physical quality post and advance notice of line changes would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask us about washdown. When robots can safely clean a dairy filler, that is when my hands-on job is really exposed. The time spent cleaning is work now, whatever the production board says.

headlineQuote: The time spent cleaning is work now, whatever the production board says.
portrait: **Wendy** Hansen, 43, runs a milk filler and capper, hears faulty lids early and holds a vocational certificate.
She and her **bus-driver** partner Tom have two school-age children, a mortgage and around four months of expenses saved.
She **uses** AI occasionally for fault codes but checks the manual and presses her union on unpaid washdown time.
**Thinking** AI changes dairy ordering before capable robots reach physical filling and cleaning in the AGI pictures.
She **seeks** paid safety training and posted bill-covering roles while building savings from extra shifts, and fast robot change alarms her.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI scenario gives too little time before robots may take her filler hours around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** training tied to a posted physical quality role and advance notice of robot-line changes would help.
